question: Does narrowing DRR's lag window to a single sample cost detections where breathing is normal but not where it is slow, as the shape of the cross-correlation predicts, in people never analysed before?

arxiv_queries: abs:"respiratory sinus arrhythmia" AND abs:"breathing rate"
abs:"heart rate variability" AND abs:elderly AND abs:respiration
literature.search: respiratory sinus arrhythmia ageing or breathing rate or cardiorespiratory cross-correlation

lineage.observation: V3D-EXP-0003 passed at ceiling: on its 190 held-out 10-minute windows a one-sample (0.25 s) lag window, which its half-period rationale rejects, detected 189 and met every criterion on real recordings. In 2-minute windows of the same people the one-sample window detected slow breathers more often than the 3 s window and normal breathers less often.

preregistration.title: Does a one-sample lag window lose normal breathers but not slow ones? (held-out Fantasia elderly windows)
preregistration.question: In a cohort never read before, does replacing DRR's 3 s lag window with a one-sample (0.25 s) window lower detection of respiration -> heart-rate coupling where breathing is normal, but not where it is slow?
preregistration.hypothesis: In held-out 2-minute windows from the Fantasia elderly cohort (seconds 60-6060 of each record), replacing the 3 s lag window with a one-sample (0.25 s) window lowers the subject-balanced detection rate of respiration -> heart-rate coupling in normal-breathing windows (dominant breathing frequency at least 0.1667 Hz) by at least 0.03, lowers it in slow-breathing windows (0.0833 Hz up to, but not including, 0.1667 Hz) by no more than 0.02, and keeps detections between mismatched people at or below 0.10 under both windows.
preregistration.rationale: V3D-EXP-0003 derived its lag window from an argument: two signals sharing a rhythm correlate most strongly once every half period, so only a window of half a period is sure to contain the peak, and a shorter window should fail most where breathing is slow. Explorations of seen young-cohort data (not evidence; the 2-minute report's hash is bound in this registration) point the other way. Detection does not need the peak, only enough correlation to beat a max-statistic null that grows with every lag searched. Slow breathing broadens the correlation peak, so a narrow window loses little there and pays no search cost; normal breathing sharpens it, so a narrow window can miss it. In 2-minute windows the one-sample window detected slow-breathing windows more often than the 3 s window (0.891 against 0.841, subject-balanced) and normal-breathing windows less often (0.890 against 0.960); in 1-minute windows the differences were +0.042 and -0.150. In 10-minute windows every lag window detected nearly every window, so no difference could show: hence 2-minute windows. The elderly cohort is twenty people no experiment has read, with weaker age-related coupling that lowers the ceiling further. If the half-period argument is right, the one-sample window loses slow breathers and F1 records it.
procedure: Explore window lengths on already-seen young-cohort data only (the tool refuses unseen bytes in exploration) and bind the 2-minute report's hash, and its rehearsal, into this registration.
Retrieve and cite literature with Anna; convene the R.A.I.N. offline panel over those sources; bind both by hash.
Register this definition after the data ledger confirms that no byte of seconds 60-6060 of any listed record has been read. Commit and push the registration before any of that data is fetched.
Fetch seconds 60-6060 of each record as one byte range, log it in the ledger, and cut it into fifty 120 s windows.

Per window: detect R peaks (5-20 Hz band-pass, 330 ms refractory); exclude the window if fewer than 20 valid RR intervals are found or the valid-RR fraction is below 0.95; resample respiration (1 Hz low-pass) and instantaneous heart rate to 4 Hz; high-pass both at 0.05 Hz; z-score.
Assign each window a stratum from respiration alone, using the dominant Welch peak f from DRR's resonance detector: slow if 0.0833 <= f < 0.1667 Hz, normal if f >= 0.1667 Hz, otherwise neither.

Test respiration -> heart rate with DRR RootingAnalyzer (lagged correlation, 199 circular-shift surrogates, max-statistic correction) under two arms with the same seed per window: lags 1-12 samples (3 s) and lag 1 sample only (0.25 s). A window is detected when its adjusted p <= 0.05.

Run the identical tests on mismatched pairs (a window's respiration with another person's heart rate from the same segment; the partner moves one person further in each segment) and on 20 synthetic AR(1) pairs each of: coupling at lag 4 samples, no coupling, coupling at lag 18 samples.

A stratum's detection rate is the unweighted mean, over people with at least one window in the stratum, of each person's share of detected windows there. Mismatched and synthetic rates are plain shares.
Submit measurements as rain-experiment-submission/v1; R.A.I.N. evaluates the criteria.

independent: lag window: 3 s vs one sample (0.25 s)
pairing: same person vs mismatched people
dependent: max-statistic adjusted p-value, respiration -> heart rate
controls: both windows on the same windows with the same seeds
synthetic coupled and independent AR(1) pairs
mismatched-person pairs from the same segment (real-data negative control)
identical preprocessing, surrogates and correction in both arms

guards.note: The data must be unseen at registration, or it confirms nothing.
And unseen when the registration was committed.
At most 400 of 1,000 windows may fail QC; ectopic beats are commoner in older people.
The 3 s window must keep its power on a known coupling.

success.note: The narrow window misses normal breathers.

failure.note: The narrow window loses slow breathers, as the half-period argument predicts.
No cost where breathing is normal: the narrow window is simply as good.

limitations: The one-sample window cannot reach the synthetic positive control (coupling at lag 4 samples) by construction, so its power is not guarded; only its false-positive rate is.
The prediction comes from explorations of a younger cohort. Older people breathe and couple differently; that difference is what this holdout tests, and it may also move the strata.
Strata come from the dominant Welch peak of a 2-minute window (about 0.03 Hz resolution); a misassigned window adds noise to both contrasts alike.
Detection means max-statistic adjusted p <= 0.05 for respiration -> heart rate. Lagged correlation ignores sign and lag 0, so this tests coupling, not direction.
Mismatched pairs share the time into the recording, and every subject watched the same film. A film-locked common response would raise mismatched detections and count against the hypothesis.
The holdout guarantee rests on this tool's data ledger: it shows no byte of these ranges was read through the pipeline before registration, and cannot rule out reads made outside it.
Literature retrieval uses Anna's deterministic hashing embeddings (lexical, not semantic) over arXiv metadata and abstracts only.
